TypeScript provides six property-manipulation utilities that look similar but operate on fundamentally different input shapes. items.title: Signing lab reports with Ed25519: why we sign a canonical record, not the PDF
items.summary: A lab report (a certificate of analysis, or COA) is a small document with a large trust problem. The lab issues a PDF. A seller posts it. A buyer reads it months later, on a page the lab does not control. A PDF can be edited in minutes, and a screenshot is easier still. We wanted a report that a stranger can check without trusting the page it sits on, and without trusting us to answer an email. This post covers the design we chose: an Ed25519 signature over a canonical data record, with the PDF tied to that record by its hash. The pattern works for any document that has to stay provable: invoices, certificates, audit exports. PDF has its own signature standard, PAdES (ETSI EN 319 142-1). The reader software shows a signature panel, and trust comes from certificates that the reader already knows. That solves a related problem, but it has costs for our case: The signature is tied to one rendering. The same results on a web page or in an API response are not covered. A check needs a PDF library that understands signatures, or a desktop reader. It is hard to do in twenty lines of code. The signed thing is a layout. items.summary: Quick answer BullMQ is a Node.js job queue backed by Redis: your web code adds a job to a queue, and a worker runs it, so slow work never blocks a web request. This post sends three shop orders through a BullMQ queue, charges the two good ones, and watches the third fail and retry because its total is missing. A customer in Karachi clicks buy on a small online shop. The checkout code charges the card, updates stock, and sends a confirmation email, all inside one web request. Then the email service stalls, the request times out, and the customer clicks buy again. The card is charged twice, and the shop owner hears about it from an angry customer, not a log. A queue breaks that chain. The web request only records the order and hands it to BullMQ, and a worker charges it and sends the email in its own time. If the worker crashes halfway, the order still sits in Redis, waiting for the next worker. My first check: does the work need to outlive the web request? items.summary: A good object storage service that supports pre-signed URLs can keep secure user file upload and download out of your application server: issue short-lived signed requests, and choose storage by the largest backup you must move, not by the upload demo that looks nicest. For a property-management system, that means the avatar upload and the nightly per-tenant backup can share a security model while using different throughput limits. Start with the transfer boundary. Keep it bounded. The useful boundary is this: your API authenticates a person and decides which object they may touch. Object storage moves the bytes. A signed URL carries that decision to the browser or backup worker for a limited operation and time window. One line, ignore-scripts=false, in a folder I had just cloned, switched my protection off, and the install gave me no sign it had happened. The marker file was the only witness. That piece ended with a question I could not answer from memory, and it came from cryptostrapon in the comments: before you install, does npm config list show you the override, and does it say where it came from? I had a guess. My guess was that it would show the final value and nothing else, a flat list with no blame attached. I ran it instead of arguing from memory, on my own machine, node v24.22.1 and npm 10.9.4, with the same test package and the same setup as yesterday: a user config saying ignore-scripts=true, a repo config saying false, and a hook that writes a marker file if it runs. My claim, before the numbers: the four-second check that would have caught yesterday's override is not a nice habit for careful people. items.title: Mongoose's November Advisories: Check sanitizeFilter and Your Version Today
items.summary: On November 10, 2026, GitHub published five security advisories for Mongoose, the MongoDB library used by a large share of Node.js backends. One is rated critical and two are rated high. Two of them concern sanitizeFilter, the setting many teams turn on to stop login-bypass style query injection. The fixes shipped in August and October. What changed this week is that the details and proof-of-concept code are public, and npm audit and Dependabot now flag old versions. If your app uses Mongoose and has not been updated since late October, check it today. A smaller item is covered at the end: node-forge had a batch of advisories published the same day. The five advisories, with the versions that fix them: Advisory Severity What goes wrong Fixed in CVE-2026-125120 Critical (CVSS 9.8) sanitizeFilter was not applied to countDocuments() 9.9.2, 8.24.3, 7.8.12, 6.13.11 CVE-2026-125119 High (7.5) sanitizeFilter set on a connection was never applied 9.11.4, 8.24.7, 7.8.13, 6.13.12 CVE-2026-125117 High (8.2) Crafted keys overwrite built-in functions and shared schema state 9.11.4, 8.24.7, 7.8.13, 6.13.12 CVE-2026-125118 Medium (6.5) Prototype pollution through Schema.prototype.virtual() 9.11.4

items.title: I shipped a habit app that only allows one habit
items.summary: Most habit apps become a second todo list. You add ten habits on day one, miss half of them on day two, and stop opening the app by day four. I shipped an iPhone app, bububaba, that refuses that loop. You start with one daily habit. Finish it, earn one water drop, and water a tree. The tree grows from sprout to sapling to mature, then you harvest fruit. Leave it too long and it wilts. A run of finished days brings it back. A second habit stays locked until you complete 30 days in a row. The app is free, English and Vietnamese, iOS 17 or later: bububaba on the App Store. I did not limit the app to one habit because the data model was hard. A list of habits is the easy version. The limit is there so the home screen can answer a single question: did I do the thing today? A Home Screen widget shows the task that is still waiting. The reminder fires at the time you choose, again near the end of the day, and when the tree is thirsty. Check-in is a tap, with an optional note and photo. That is the whole daily path. items.title: Day 25: The Audit Trail and the Before and After Values of a Change
items.summary: By the time someone asks who changed the amount on this record last month, it is usually months later. Whoever is asking has neither the screen as it looked then nor the build that was running, only the few rows left behind at the time. Who logged in, who changed which field from what to what, who looked at which record: every decision in the auditing layer has to assume that scene first, including the ones that look like nothing more than saving space. This post covers: Why the name is copied in as well, rather than storing an id and joining back for it How one column encodes the whole outcome of a login, and why the failure reason is kept apart from the line shown to the user Why the access record covers only single record reads, and why it is the one of the three that is off by default Why a change is one row per save, why that write sits outside the transaction, and what happens when it fails How what changed is stored as a DiffGram, and why there is only one place it can be captured Recording every call is not workable. items.title: Estados de email accesibles en React
items.summary: Un formulario de registro puede parecer terminado cuando el usuario pulsa “Crear cuenta”. En realidad, ahí empieza una parte delicada: enviar el email, esperar la respuesta, mostrar el resultado y permitir que la persona continúe sin adivinar qué ocurrió. En proyectos React he encontrado que este flujo se trata aveces como un detalle visual. Un spinner aparece, el botón se desactiva y, si todo va bien, llega un mensaje verde. Ese enfoque falla cuando el correo tarda, cuando el usuario navega con teclado o cuando un lector de pantalla no recibe el cambio. La interfaz necesita un modelo de estados explícito, no solo una animación. Un estado de email tiene al menos cinco momentos útiles: Inicial: todavía no se ha enviado nada. Enviando: la petición está en curso y no debe duplicarse. Esperando: el servidor aceptó la solicitud, pero el mensaje aún no ha sido confirmado. Verificado: el enlace fue aceptado y el flujo puede continuar. Error: la persona necesita una explicación y una acción posible. Separar “enviando” de “esperando” mejora la experiencia. items.summary: timob58 shares a report from TechCrunch: Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable. The change, which will roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks, marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period mentioned in Google's Gemini Apps Privacy Hub, according to an archived version from November 12. OpenAI, by comparison, says it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed, instead pointing to a blog post that says chats are kept longer to respond to users, process feedback, and protect its services and users. Its updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models. The malware replaced cryptocurrency addresses, attempted to steal credit card information and cookies, and sought to compromise iOS devices. Websites belonging to at least 178 organizations were affected via the "OPTIMJACK" vulnerability, which has since been patched. "Earlier today, Optimizely identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects," the company said. "We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered." items.title: IAsyncEnumerable Streaming
items.summary: Streaming" width="800" height="1000"> During a recent performance audit of our reporting APIs, I tracked down erratic Gen2 GC pauses to a seemingly innocent endpoint. The code called .ToListAsync() on a massive table containing over 50,000 historical transaction records before returning an Ok(list) response. This approach forces ASP.NET Core to allocate the entire result set in memory, doubling or tripling allocations during JSON serialization and locking up thread pool resources. [HttpGet("reports")] public async Task GetReports() { var list = await db.Orders.ToListAsync(); return Ok(list); // buffers all rows in RAM } By leveraging IAsyncEnumerable straight from Entity Framework Core, we bypass the intermediate list allocation entirely. The ASP.NET Core framework understands this interface and immediately streams the records down the HTTP response pipe as data flows from the underlying SQL Server data reader. [HttpGet("reports")] public IAsyncEnumerable GetReports() { return db.Orders.AsAsyncEnumerable(); } Heap Allocations: Bypasses temporary List backing arrays, keeping memory usage flat regardless of row count. items.title: The tests were green, a person found the hole: a vulnerability in our OpenID server, start to finish
items.summary: How many green tests does it take to believe a protection works? We have about two thousand, and they pass on three databases. A person still found the hole: an outside researcher who worked through our server and saw a connection where we had seen none. This is the story of GHSA-vmj2-8phj-mfxf in redb.Identity, our OAuth 2.1 / OpenID Connect server for .NET. In order and with dates: what was broken, why we did not see it ourselves, how we fixed it and how we disclosed it. On 4 November a private report on version 4.6.1 came in. Its author, Rathnadeepan (HotWater, HotWater-015 on GitHub), did not open a public issue or write a blog post about it. He wrote to us directly and left us time to fix it. We checked the report against the source the same day. It was all true. A plain access token is accepted from anyone who presents it. If it is stolen from a log, a proxy or an intermediate node, it can be used. DPoP (RFC 9449) changes that by binding the token to the client's key. The token carries the key's thumbprint (cnf.jkt), and with every request the client sends a short proof signed by that key: method, URL, time, a one-time identifier and the hash of the token itself. items.title: Building a Resume Editor That Exports Real Text: A4 Layout, Vector PDFs and DOCX
items.summary: On paper, building a resume editor sounds like a weekend project. You throw together a two-column layout: form inputs on the left, a live preview on the right, and a shiny "Download PDF" button up top. Simple, right? Except it almost never is. The moment a user actually relies on your tool to apply for a job, expectations skyrocket. They expect the exported file to mirror the on-screen preview pixel for pixel. They expect it to fit neatly onto standard A4 paper without awkward blank gaps. They want the typography intact. And most importantly: they expect the output to be a living, breathing document—one with selectable, copyable text that applicant tracking systems (ATS) can actually parse, and maybe even a Word (.docx) file they can tweak later. While building Pagewise, I quickly realized a fundamental truth that reshaped how I approached the entire architecture: A document that looks great in a web browser isn’t guaranteed to survive printing, PDF parsing, or external word processors. items.summary: The 3 AM Page: When Preview Chrome Becomes Render Artifact You wake to an alert: the automated video pipeline produced 47 corrupted exports overnight. Frame one shows your application's sidebar. Frame twelve captures a modal mid-transition. The encoder did exactly what you asked—it rendered the HTML you gave it, including the preview interface you forgot was part of the DOM tree. This is the failure mode I am addressing while evaluating heygen-com/hyperframes. Its premise, "Write HTML. Render video," makes HTML the production artifact. A preview dialog, responsive sidebar, or entrance animation must never quietly become part of that artifact. For a React application using Tailwind CSS v4 and Radix primitives, my recommendation is straightforward: isolate the render document, and animate only the surrounding interface. The architecture has three responsibilities. The application produces a self-contained HTML document. The preview interface displays that document without modifying it. A render adapter submits the same document, together with explicit viewport and timing settings, to the video-rendering workflow. That adapter is where Hyperframes integration belongs. items.title: School Phone Bans Are Gradually Improving Test Scores
items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: School cellphone bans are beginning to modestly improve students' academic performance, according to the first large national analysis that compared students' test scores before and after the bans. Schools with strict bans -- requiring students to lock their phones in pouches all school day -- saw math and reading scores improve as if students had an additional week or two of school a year, the study found. It was published Tuesday by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard. U.S. students' test scores began falling over a decade ago. The drop coincided with the rise of smartphones, raising questions about their role in the decline. The evidence so far on the academic effects of phone bans has been mixed. But the new study indicates they are starting to have an influence. The study looked at 3.3 million students between 2021 and 2026. They were in third through 10th grade, attending 4,600 U.S. schools. Using scores on MAP tests, which track achievement from fall to spring, it compared the performance of students at schools that put in strict phone bans with those at similar schools that did not have such bans.

items.title: BugMeNot Calls It Quits
items.summary: BugMeNot, the password-sharing service launched in 2003 to help users bypass website registration requirements, has shut down without explanation after more than two decades. All that's left on the website is a farewell message that reads: "Thanks to everyone who envisioned a better internet." heise online reports: Founded by Guy King, the service had been online since 2003: BugMeNot was a collection of login credentials for various online services. Volunteers submitted credentials they had created for different websites. The idea was simple: Nobody wants to create a full account and provide all their sensitive information just to use a service occasionally. Two decades ago, this privacy concern was more firmly embedded in the public consciousness, but it has since faded considerably. Back then, usernames and passwords were usually the only access controls, so people could easily submit those credentials. Multifactor authentication was still exotic, and passkeys were a distant prospect. The once-popular service lost its shine after just a few years. items.title: Muting the mic for every app on macOS with Core Audio
items.summary: Zoom, Teams and Meet each have their own mute, and they don't know about each other. I wanted one hotkey that mutes the mic for everything, so I made a small menu bar app for it. It sets kAudioDevicePropertyMute on the input devices through Core Audio, so every app just gets silence. By default it mutes all inputs, not only the default one, because Zoom and Meet often disagree about which mic is "the" mic. It also listens for changes and puts the mute back if some app flips it. ⌘⇧M toggles it, and there's push to talk too. Later I added optional local recording of the mic plus system audio into one small file, which is handy for dropping a call into ChatGPT or Claude for a summary. It's free and MIT, macOS 14+: github.com/oochernyshev/lockmic. I'm the developer, happy to answer Core Audio questions.

The first version answered "how do I find a tag fast". Since then it has gone through five releases in one week, driven by feedback: XPath 1.0, CSS selectors, a review against hostile markup, and parsing straight from a char[] buffer. items.title: How to check a license key in your Mac app offline
items.summary: Short answer: Sign each license on your server with Ed25519, then verify it in the app with CryptoKit and the matching public key. Honest customers stay unlocked offline, because the check does not need a network call. Verify the signature and the expiry at launch and again where the paid feature runs, not in a single isLicensed() flag. A shared serial list, or a secret compiled into the app, can be copied out of the binary. Anyone who has that secret can invent keys your app will accept, or share one serial widely. AI tools make that read faster than it used to be. A signed license works the other way around. Your server holds a private key and signs a small payload: the customer's email, the product name, and an expiry. The app ships the public key and uses it to verify the signature. System.Threading.Channels makes you pick one of those, which is exactly what it should do. items.summary: I'm Zak, and I build InkHammy, a grammar checker that runs as a Mac menu bar app and as an iPhone keyboard. Disclosure up front: InkHammy is my product. This post isn't a review; it's a write-up of how the Mac app reads and fixes text inside other apps through the macOS Accessibility API, and the design choices that came out of it. A browser extension only sees web pages. A lot of writing on a Mac happens somewhere else: Slack, Mail, Notes, Messages, the ChatGPT app, and text fields inside desktop apps built on web views. To check text in all of them, an app has to follow whichever field has focus, read its text, know where each word sits on screen, and write corrections back without breaking the host app. macOS exposes this through the Accessibility API (AX). The user grants Accessibility permission once in System Settings, and the app can then observe and act on UI elements in other processes. AX is powerful, but every host app implements it a little differently, and a call into a busy app can block. Most of InkHammy's Mac architecture exists to deal with those two facts. items.title: Why I took Whisper out of my iPhone transcription app before it shipped
items.summary: I work on Koedori at W Lab. It is an iPhone app that records a lecture, a meeting or an interview and turns it into text on the phone itself, with no account, and the audio is never uploaded. The early builds ran Whisper through WhisperKit. The version on the App Store has no Whisper in it at all: it uses Apple's SpeechAnalyzer framework and its SpeechTranscriber module. This post is about why, and what building on SpeechTranscriber is like. Koedori makes three promises: transcription is free and needs no account, audio never leaves the phone, and re-transcribing costs nothing, as often as you like. The second one is architecture, not a setting. There is no code path that uploads audio, and the app has no server of its own. So recognition has to run on the device, and it has to be cheap enough to run again on a whim. Whisper on the phone met that on paper. The trouble was everything around the model. WhisperKit compiles a model for the Neural Engine the first time it loads it. On the iPhone 14 I measured, the first load of large-v3 turbo after an install took 197 to 205 seconds, every time. A reload within the same install took 4 seconds, and a 10-second clip then transcribed in 0.

items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Just 400 hyperscale data centers connected in the US used as much electricity as the state of Michigan in a single year, new Harvard research has found. The study, published Monday in Nature Sustainability, also finds that the majority of that electricity was generated using fossil fuels, and data center emissions are three times higher than they were before the AI boom. Federal and state governments do not track data center use separate from the rest of the power sector, despite mounting projections that data centers are putting serious strain on the American power grid. Individual data centers' power use is often considered proprietary business information, and data center operators and utilities do not have to disclose specific numbers to the public. The Harvard study specifically focuses on hyperscale data centers -- the largest types of facilities, which have become flashpoints in community opposition across the country. items.summary: I kept doing the same thing ten times a day: copy a Slack message into a chat window, ask for "more professional" or "shorter", copy the answer, paste it back. So I built Quill, a small macOS menu bar app that does the round trip for me. Select text in any app, press ⌃⌥Space, pick a prompt, and the rewrite replaces your selection. Undo still works, because Quill pastes through the app's own paste. Prompts: Fix Grammar, Professional, Shorter and Friendly to start. You can add, edit, reorder and delete them, or type a one-off instruction. Direct shortcuts: any prompt can have its own global shortcut, which rewrites the selection without opening the popup. No selection: Quill rewrites the whole text field. Model: it uses your own Groq API key with openai/gpt-oss-20b. It's written in SwiftUI and AppKit, with no third-party dependencies, and needs macOS 14 or later. The hard part isn't the AI call. It's reading and writing text in someone else's app, safely. Quill registers system-wide hotkeys with Carbon, which still works, and needs no extra permission for this. One shortcut opens the popup. Each prompt can have its own. items.title: Your iOS App Says “Offline”—But Is It? Debugging API Failures With a VPN Enabled
items.summary: A user connects their iPhone to a VPN, opens your app and sees: No internet connection. Please try again. They switch to another app, which works. Your app may have encountered a real failure. But “no internet” might be the wrong diagnosis. A hostname lookup can fail. A secure connection can fail. An API can return an authentication error. The response can arrive successfully and then fail JSON decoding. A failed API operation does not automatically mean the device is offline—or that the VPN caused the failure. The first useful fix is to preserve those distinctions in your networking code. Think of an API operation as several stages: Establish a usable network connection. Resolve the destination hostname when needed. Establish the secure connection. Exchange the HTTP request and response. Interpret the response body. This is a debugging model, not a claim that every request creates a new connection or performs a fresh DNS lookup. Connections and lookup results can be reused. The point is that failures at different stages need different handling. items.title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic (15 minute read)
items.summary: A floating-point number stores a fixed number of significant digits and a separate exponent. When two numbers with very different exponents are added, the small one has to be shifted to line up with the big one, and the digits that fall off on the end are gone. That means that (a+b)+c is not always equal to a+(b+c). This post looks at what happens when integer addition, which is exact, is used.

items.title: Handing over humanity (22 minute read)
items.summary: Some AI experts believe that once we achieve superintelligence, humans will be permanently disempowered, and we shall all be ruled by an AI god. This might not be such a desirable outcome, as humans have a natural desire for freedom. The arrangement will probably not work, as keeping power responsive to human needs has required checks developed over centuries, sustained by repeated feedback from the real world and correction, and there's no reason to keep that equilibrium stable once humans have surrendered all control. Humans have the ability now to steer the technology in a way that will not lead to a complete replacement of human judgment.

items.title: LLMs can learn some multi-step reasoning on filler tokens instead of visible CoT (9 minute read)
items.summary: By changing the training setup and applying LoRAs to Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and gpt-oss-20b, researchers taught models to do some multi-step tasks while emitting only filler tokens, beating an answer-only baseline on three of seven tasks. The work is meant to separate filler-token reasoning from steganographic hidden reasoning when interpreting chain-of-thought.

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.

items.title: Apple Cuts Internal AI Usage Budgets in Move to Reduce Spending (5 minute read)
items.summary: Apple quietly lowered the daily spending cap on AI models for its employees last month. Some engineers had their budgets cut from $300 to $200, and the company is planning further cuts for some engineering teams that may potentially reduce their daily allowances to as little as $100. Groups outside of engineering may have their limits reduced to $25 from $100. Employees say that few workers were using their full $300 daily allowances, making the previous limits unnecessarily generous.

items.title: The Stacks Project, formalized in Lean (13 minute read)
items.summary: Axiom has released a Lean formalization of the entire Stacks Project. The Stacks project is an open-source reference that lays the foundation of modern algebraic geometry. The release is the largest integrated, reusable library of formalized mathematics ever built. It makes the full mathematical development of the Stacks Project available as a single, machine-checked library that researchers and AI agents can import from directly into new formal proofs.

items.title: Rebuilding the global town square from scratch (32 minute read)
items.summary: The new version of X.com's web app was built by five engineers working with AI coding agents in under six months. It loads pages significantly faster than the old web app over slow connections, and it already serves logged-out users and the pages that search engines crawl. This post covers why X.com was rebuilt, how the new web app is being rolled out, and how the old and new apps compare today. It also looks at the performance work completed since logged-out traffic moved over.
